title: Renewal in Christ
english: As farmers, we are called to proceed to our works because it is fitting to do so.
The meadows produce a varied appearance of flowers.
The plants in the fields and gardens produce growth, just like rabbits produce their own kind, demonstrating the power of nature to bring forth life.
Children are already green, a reminder of God's philanthropy, and the scripture says, 'Producing grass for the animals' (Psalm 104:14).
The law has not ordered us to observe the month of the new moons in vain, but rather so that we may see the usefulness of the commandment, which is to proceed to works.
Human nature should strive to be in competition with the fields that produce green growth, and with the growths of piety that bloom around us.

Let us bring to ourselves the power that changes things, and having transferred the purpose of our thoughts to what is useful, let us see carefully if our word will fail to be fitting, calling the time of the Savior's visitation the month of the new moons, on which it is fitting for all to celebrate.

Then, in addition to these things, the given firstfruits of the Spirit, like a gentle breeze or a soft wind, blows around all souls, covering those in whom it dwells with a fragrance that is not inferior, skillfully preparing them.
For we are the fragrance of Christ to God, as Paul says (2 Corinthians 2:15).
And we have cast off the oldness of our past life like a leaf, and we are being renewed into a new and fresh citizenship.
Thus, the blessed Paul also said: If anyone is in Christ, they are a new creation, the old things have passed away, behold, all things have become new (2 Corinthians 5:17).

But if someone thinks that through the divine Scripture, they have not strayed far from the truth, let them hear the words of the bridegroom, who signals the true month of the new moon to the bride, saying: 'Arise, come, my dove, my beautiful one, for behold, the winter has passed, the rain has gone, the flowers have appeared on the earth, the time of pruning has arrived' (Song of Solomon 2:10-13).

For just as those who have knowledge of cultivating the earth, prudently cut off the useless branches of the vine, but allow the ones that are suitable for fruit-bearing to remain, so also our all-wise God, examining each mind, cuts off the idle and, as it were, hardened counsels, but allows the sober thought to be set free, to be saved, and to remain.

From here we are being led to salvation, having sent away the passions of the flesh, and having settled the pure grace of the Spirit within ourselves, we are being transformed into a better citizenship, and we remember the words of Paul, saying: our old man was crucified, so that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we might no longer be slaves to sin (Romans 6:6).
For he who has died has been freed from sin.
If we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with Him (Romans 6:8).

We will truly live and reign with Him, turning away from the defilement of the body and hating it, and hating, as one of the saints says, the tunic defiled by the flesh, and the dark cloud of sin's gloom has been lifted through grace.
We honor the self-control loved by God, offering a life of virtue as a gift to Christ who died for us.
The Psalmist also said: all those around Him will bring gifts (Psalm 76:11).
What then will our gift to the Lord be, or in what way will it be offered, and how will it be acceptable, it is worthy to investigate and learn from the divine Scripture.
He says: if a soul offers a gift, a sacrifice to the Lord, its gift will be semolina, and it will pour oil on it and put frankincense on it, making it a true sacrifice.
The grains of semolina, ground into one bread, signify the multitude of virtues that make up one piety, which is offered to God as a sacrifice and gift in order.
The oil poured on it is a symbol of joy, reminding us that we should not be gloomy in our pursuit of virtue, but rather joyful and grateful for the gift of salvation.
As we rejoice in the hope of struggling against sin, we must consider the nature of our actions and their consequences.

The Lebanon, being trodden upon, reveals the fragrance that arises from our works, demonstrating the importance of purity and the need to turn away from evil pleasures, and to desire the boast of purity.
To achieve this, it is necessary to be outside all impurity and to desire the boast of purity, which would make our incense offering acceptable to God.
If someone wanted to offer a gift to a notable person, they would not dare to approach with a dirty body, as this would be detestable and arrogant.

Similarly, when offering ourselves to God, we must ensure that our thoughts and actions are proper and in line with the divine law, which states that every sacrifice offered to God should not be leavened, and that no leaven or honey should be offered from it (Leviticus 2:11).
Instead, we should offer the firstfruits and salt our sacrifices, as the salt of the Lord's covenant should not cease from our offerings.
To become the new dough, we must cleanse the old leaven, for we are unleavened, as Paul says (1 Corinthians 5:7).
The Lord will not accept the stench of evil from our old nature, for He seeks a new and sincere life from us.
The pleasure of sin may seem sweet, but its end is bitter, and we must reject it, just as we reject the approach of honey, which signifies pleasure.
We must strive to please God, not by pursuing a life of shame and pleasure, but by doing what is right in His sight.
This is why He commands us to salt our sacrifices, introducing a symbol of reason and understanding.
By seasoning our minds with divine fear, we can prevent them from flowing out towards shameful desires and easily turning to what is worse.
As Paul says, our speech should be seasoned with salt (Colossians 4:6).
But first, we must have our thoughts in order, for it is from the abundance of the heart that the mouth speaks (Matthew 12:34).
Let the minds of the devout be seasoned with salt, and let sin flow away like something superfluous, and not be softened, carried away by shameful pleasures.
To become steadfast and unmovable, always abounding in the Lord's work, is the ultimate goal, for those who are not yet firmly established and have a secure mind are far from all praise.
Our Master also reproaches us through the prophet, saying that they loved to move their feet and did not spare, and God was not pleased with them.
The feet signify a kind of transitional movement and the inclination of the mind to either side, to the worthless things, and to the things that demand admiration.
The prophet says, 'He set my feet on a rock' (Psalm 40:2), signifying the firm and unchangeable disposition that we should strive for.
The apostle Paul exhorts us to abound in the Lord's work, according to human nature, and to be inseparable from the divine love.
By doing so, we can ensure that our feet are firmly planted on the rock of faith, and we can avoid the transitional movement that leads to worthless things.

title: The Law of the Whole Burnt Offering
english: It is through good works that one's true character is revealed. A sound mind would not lead someone to abandon divine laws at times, only to return to them later as if waking up from a sleep. This behavior is comparable to those who fall off a ship in the middle of the sea and are tossed about by waves. Having escaped the initial fear, they neglect their safety and only realize what is useful when they are in the midst of evil. Then, they try to swim back to the ship, seeking safety from the very place they fell.

One should not wait for the end of danger to arrive, but rather hate it before it comes. This approach would be more sound. If it seems to everyone that imitating those who accept such things is full of foolishness, and they marvel at what is rightly censured, then they should bring all eagerness to be guided by divine laws and offer a blameless way of life. And if anyone, seeing the foolishness of such a thing, accepts the imitation of those who do this, how should they not bring all eagerness to be possessed by divine laws and offer a blameless polity? Hear again what the divine law proclaims to us about these things: "And the Lord spoke, saying, 'Command Aaron and his sons: This is the law of the whole burnt offering. This is the whole burnt offering upon the altar, all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn upon it, it shall not be extinguished'" (Leviticus 6:8-13).

As we have been encouraged by the grace of our Savior, we can approach God with confidence, and it is this confidence that allows us to understand the importance of devotion to Him. The Word of God, which is philanthropic in nature, draws all people to piety and encourages them to live virtuous lives, stirring up those who are obedient to His laws to strive for excellence. However, not everyone has the same level of enthusiasm for this, and each person is led by their own unique eagerness.

Some individuals are more diligent in their approach to God, considering nothing more important than their devotion to Him, and they offer themselves as a whole and undivided sacrifice to the Lord. This is what it means to be a whole burnt offering, where one offers themselves entirely to God, without any reservation or evil intent. The law of the whole burnt offering says: "This is the whole burnt offering, all night upon the altar until morning. And the fire of the altar shall burn upon it, it shall not be extinguished" (Leviticus 6:12-13). This fire can be seen as a symbol of the Holy Spirit's presence in us, which the Savior referred to when He said, "I came to cast fire on the earth" (Luke 12:49). The one who is wholly devoted to God should strive to keep this inextinguishable fire burning within them, always having the power of the holy flame in their life, for the whole night, which represents the present life.

The mind must be continually rekindled, and there should be a single, unwavering approach to spiritual life, always zealous in spirit, as Paul teaches. By examining the law carefully, we can gain a deeper understanding of God's will, and this is made clearer through various examples. For instance, God instructs the high priest Moses on the proper way to offer sacrifices on the altar.

The command to offer two year-old lambs on the altar every day, one in the morning and one in the evening, along with a specific amount of fine flour mixed with oil and wine, signifies the importance of continuous worship and honor to God. This ritual encompasses all time, from the beginning to the end of each day, and reminds us that no moment should pass without acknowledging and honoring God. The use of wine, oil, and fine flour in the offering also holds significance, as it represents the fragrance of good works that we are to offer to God continually, like a perpetual sacrifice. Through a certain riddle, teaching that those who continually offer honor to God, and as it were bring a sacrifice to the lawgiver with greater fervor, having been pitied, will rejoice, having received a small part of the gift in the present life, but in the future age, the fullness of grace will be given to them, when, as the prophet says, "Eternal joy will be over their heads, and pain and sighing will flee" (Isaiah 35:10). The law commands us not to deviate from the right path, and if we neglect such good things, we will be liable for all punishment.

If one considers human nature, it seems that the tone of such conduct is difficult, but the law shows a way of life that is easier than what was said, and more attainable. The law provides a solution to the problem of human weakness, and it is possible to follow it without being overwhelmed by its demands.

When God appeared to the sons of Israel in fire, darkness, and storm, and established laws regarding their actions, Moses, thinking it necessary to show them the type of polity pleasing to the lawgiver through a clear deed, did something remarkable. He rose early, built an altar under the mountain, and sent young men to offer whole burnt offerings and sacrifices of salvation to God. This act was a demonstration of the kind of benefit that appears to us from this event.

Moses' rising early and building an altar teaches us that it is necessary to awaken as if from sleep and rise to sobriety, having passed through the cloud of sin like a dark night, and now running towards the light of knowledge. By doing so, we establish our own mind as a good altar to God, a concept also expressed by the prophet Isaiah when he said, "My spirit rises from the night towards you, God, because your commandments are light on the earth" (Isaiah 26:9). This is the significance of Moses' rising early, a symbol of our own spiritual awakening and growth.

As we follow the sequence of thought, we proceed to the arrangement of what is being sought. The placement of the altar, not on the mountain but under it, signifies the humble mindset of those who are still lacking in perfection and are not yet able to ascend to the heights of perfect commandments, but are near to them. This indicates that they have approached God, albeit in a state of humility.

The presence of twelve stones around the altar, corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel, teaches us that we ought to always be present with God, never falling into sinful behavior. The Psalmist declares this to us more clearly, saying: "I will encircle your altar, Lord" (Psalm 87:1). After this, he says again: "He sent out the young men of the sons of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed a salvation sacrifice to God, calves" (Leviticus 1:3). This emphasizes the importance of a youthful and noble-minded approach to offering sacrifices to God.

It is not the task of the sluggish or weak-minded to offer sacrifices to God, but rather of the youthful and noble-minded. For this reason, the young men are said to have been sent, and they offer a salvation sacrifice, calves. This highlights the significance of a strong and virtuous mindset in our relationship with God.

title: Virtue and Spiritual Growth
english: As the thing undergoes a transformation, the choice of those who bring it is commendable, yet weaker and less perfect, for what is being brought is not a full-grown ox, but a calf, lacking in size and strength compared to the perfect ox.

The blood is being divided, with half being poured into a bowl and half onto the altar, symbolizing the division of the life of the one serving, which is a mysterious division, with the blood representing the soul, whose life is divided equally with us by God, so that we do not live only for ourselves, but also keep the share of the altar.

This middle and moderate life is one that does not have a harsh and intense character, nor does it fall into sins due to excessive indulgence, but rather, it has risen to a higher level through caution and is compared to the more perfect ones, although it is lacking in eagerness.

As the habit and the quality mentioned are combined into one, a noble and gentle way of life is revealed, one that eliminates what causes pain in each and relaxes the tone of precision in the plainness of indulgence, and the excess of indulgence is cut off, like a pruning knife cutting off the harshness from the mind, and it will show the straight and blameless way of life.

It is good, therefore, to strive for what is better and to pursue virtue more, as Paul says, each of us has a gift from God, and the creator of all things, being good, provides opportunities for salvation to those who are weaker.

He considers worthy of greater praise those who strive for more perfect things, and he does not deprive of his philanthropy those who do not possess much virtue, just as human faces are not identical, so the minds of humans are not alike, and the nature of the body is one, and it is perfected through the same parts, but the difference in characters brings about change in each person.

Similarly, the mind, through the same activities, is equal in all, but it is divided into inequality by the qualities of habits, which is also illustrated by the evangelical parable of the sower, which shows that the soil is good, but the difference in fruit is irregular (Matthew 13:1-23).

The number one hundred represents those who are perfect in virtue and have reached the highest piety, while the number sixty represents those who have made some progress and possess a significant amount of virtue, and the thirty, who are still inferior, are not outside the best land, nor are they deprived of giving fruit, even if they fall short of the perfect and the smallest.

They are in the third order of those in virtue, and their reward is proportional to their labor, for many mansions are with the Father, as the Savior says (John 14:2), determining the measure of honor due to each.

The distribution of talents to the servants is a prime example of this principle, where to one, five talents were given; to another, two; to another, one, although nature is equal to all, and has the suitable word for the house, and towards perfection, no difference should be defined in these, but all should be given the five talents equally.

However, the irregularity of the gift brings a certain inequality of conditions, not receiving piety in equal measure, and the one who received the five talents heard the words of praise and encouragement from the lord, and was set over many, entering into the joy of their lord (Matthew 25:21).

In contrast, the one who received two talents also received equal praise and was honored with the same vote, demonstrating that God is not unjust, but rather good and loving honor, for the kindness towards the one who has fallen short will not diminish the honors for the more perfect, nor will it add what is due to them to the less perfect.

The idea that being envied by others for their good deeds is somehow a restriction on our freedom is a misguided one, for it is not as if the measure of virtue is applied equally to all, with the measure of grace being balanced against the life lived by each individual, as if by scales.

Rather, we should listen to the words of our Savior Christ, who says, 'Friend, I am not unjust to you, did I not agree with you for a denarius? Take what is yours and go, but I want to give to this last one as I gave to you' (Matthew 20:13-15).

This is a call to action, a reminder that we should strive to do good works and not be lazy in our pursuit of virtue, as Paul says, we should rouse our will to every good work and shake off the laziness that can so easily beset us (Ephesians 5:14).

We should rise from our spiritual slumber and lift our eyes to the sun of righteousness, knowing that our Master is a philanthropic one who will receive us with mercy and compassion, even when we have fallen short.

The Lord instructed Moses to throw his staff on the ground, and it became a snake, causing Moses to flee in fear, but when the Lord told Moses to seize the snake by its tail, it transformed back into a staff.
This miraculous event taught Moses that those who had been infected with the Egyptian plague and had strayed into sin could be transformed into piety through the honor of the Divine.

Just as a staff can sprout from the earth, but becomes a venomous snake when it turns away from the passions of the flesh, so too can humans become bitter towards sin and terrible towards wrath when they fall away from the lawgiver's guidance.
Nevertheless, when the lawgiver takes them back, they can be transformed into a good model of the best habit, and their face can be restored to its original state.
The voices of the prophets also testify to this, counseling those who sin to turn back to God from above and below, and it is not a matter of contention for us.
The Lord says, 'Do not fear me, or will you not be cautious before my face? The one who set a boundary for the sea, a perpetual decree, and it will not cross it' (Jeremiah 5:22).
However, this people had a disobedient and unresponsive heart, and they turned away, departing without saying in their heart, 'Let us fear the Lord our God' (Jeremiah 5:24).
Sometimes, the Lord rebuked them more sharply, saying, 'If the Ethiopian changes his skin or the leopard its spots, will you be able to do good, having learned evil things?' (Jeremiah 13:23).
The father of all sin had dominated the race to such an extent that there were very few who honored God and needed to remember the lawgiver they had known.

The Lord's words are a call to repentance, and we should heed them, for our Master is a philanthropic one who will receive us with mercy and compassion, even when we have fallen short, and it is not a matter of contention for us, for it is clear to everyone that God raises up again and changes the one who has slipped into sin due to laziness.

As Paul says, we should rouse our will to every good work, and shake off the laziness that can so easily beset us, and rise from our spiritual slumber, and lift our eyes to the sun of righteousness, and Christ will shine on us, for even if we have fallen asleep as humans, having been overcome by sin, now is the time to wake up for salvation, and the Master, being philanthropic, will receive us, will have mercy on us, and will not turn away from our tears, but will show us to be pure, repentant, and will restore us to piety.
